clinicalPearls: Most commonly caused by variants in SGCE (epsilon-sarcoglycan), inherited autosomal dominantly with maternal imprinting, so penetrance depends on parent of origin (usually manifest only when inherited from the father)
Core phenotype combines lightning-like myoclonic jerks, predominantly of the upper body and arms, with milder dystonia (often cervical dystonia or writer's cramp)
Onset is typically in childhood or adolescence, and the myoclonus is usually the more disabling feature
A characteristic and well-recognised feature is marked, if temporary, improvement of myoclonus with alcohol, which can lead to alcohol misuse
Psychiatric comorbidity is common, including anxiety, obsessive-compulsive features, and depression
The disorder is non-degenerative with normal cognition and structural imaging, and course is generally benign and non-progressive
Symptomatic treatment may target myoclonus and dystonia; deep brain stimulation is an option in severely affected, refractory cases
Diagnosis is supported by the clinical picture and family history and confirmed by SGCE molecular testing, keeping imprinting in mind when interpreting inheritance
reference.pathophysiology: Myoclonus-dystonia is most often caused by loss-of-function variants in SGCE, encoding epsilon-sarcoglycan, a transmembrane protein widely expressed in neurons including cerebellar Purkinje cells and monoaminergic neurons. SGCE is maternally imprinted, so only the paternally inherited allele is normally expressed, which explains why the disorder typically manifests when the variant is inherited from the father. Deficiency of epsilon-sarcoglycan is thought to disrupt cerebellothalamocortical and striatal network function, producing subcortical myoclonus and dystonia without neurodegeneration, consistent with the normal cognition and imaging.
additionalDifferentials: Essential tremor and other tremor syndromes
Progressive myoclonic epilepsies and other myoclonus syndromes
Cortical myoclonus from other neurological disease
additionalInvestigations: SGCE molecular genetic testing, interpreted with attention to maternal imprinting
Neurophysiological studies (EMG with back-averaging) to characterise the myoclonus as subcortical
Brain MRI, expected to be normal, to exclude structural or degenerative causes
Serum copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude Wilson disease when the picture is atypical
redFlags: Development of alcohol dependence driven by self-medication of myoclonus
Severe psychiatric symptoms including suicidal ideation
Atypical progression, cognitive decline, or additional neurological signs suggesting another diagnosis
Disabling myoclonus or dystonia refractory to medical therapy
reference.prognosis: The condition is generally benign and non-progressive, compatible with a normal lifespan and preserved cognition, though myoclonus and dystonia can cause functional and social disability and psychiatric comorbidity may be significant. Selected refractory patients benefit from deep brain stimulation.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the inheritance by ignoring maternal imprinting and wrongly excluding the diagnosis in an unaffected carrier parent
Overlooking or inadvertently reinforcing alcohol misuse arising from symptom self-treatment
Labelling the jerks as tics or a functional disorder without neurophysiology or genetic testing
Failing to address the frequently associated psychiatric comorbidity
management: Treat disabling myoclonus with clonazepam or other benzodiazepines, considering anticholinergics or sodium valproate as adjuncts
Manage focal dystonia such as cervical dystonia or writer's cramp with botulinum toxin injections
Offer pallidal deep brain stimulation for medically refractory, disabling myoclonus-dystonia
Counsel against using alcohol for symptom relief and screen for and manage alcohol misuse
Identify and treat psychiatric comorbidity, including anxiety, obsessive-compulsive features and depression
Provide genetic counselling for the SGCE variant, explaining maternal imprinting and parent-of-origin penetrance
Refer to a movement-disorder specialist for diagnosis and ongoing management
